extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and writing police- and crime-related news items: short incident reports, multi-incident chronicles, human-interest crime features, and capture/arrest narratives for newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report basic incident facts (who, what, when, where, how, outcome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the essential facts of the incident: the persons involved, the act committed, the date/time, precise location, manner of injury or death, and immediate outcome (arrest, hospital, death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text: named victims and suspects (e.g., 'Mario Ippolito shot down and killed'), specific dates (January 9, January 11, etc.), addresses (321 East 109th street), and outcomes (died, not fatal, taken to the Morgue, held without bail). Use concise factual statements that establish the core of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include eyewitness and participant statements/quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use direct quotations from witnesses, participants, or involved officials to convey first-hand perspective and specific claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter includes many direct quotes (e.g., Mr. Wilkins's account of Grew; Grew's statement 'I had the revolver in my right hand...'; Mrs. Grew and Gene's mother's remarks). Quotes are used to show motive, state of mind, and personal reaction—include attribution (who said it) and relevant context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide background and context (prior incidents, relationships, motive clues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Situate the incident with relevant history: prior complaints, arrests, business failures, relationships between parties, or patterns of behavior that help explain the current event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Grew's business failure and prior complaint of abuse; references to previous weekly murders in Little Italy; the escaped convict's prior record at Joliet. Background can be brief but should illuminate motive or pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detail physical evidence and scene description
rubrics_metrics.description: Report on physical items and forensic signs found at the scene (weapons, blood, money, damaged property) and observable scene details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text examples: the stiletto 'bent double', 'a pool of blood', bullets/thrusts in organs, 'three dirty glasses and an empty wine bottle', a dog that might have recognized the murderer. Such details support accounts and can rebut robbery/motive assumptions (e.g., money left in pockets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid scene-setting and narrative detail where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ descriptive, narrative passages to recreate the scene and action for the reader while remaining factual—show movement, sounds, and timing to make the reporting engaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated in the Montclair shooting and other pieces: running, panting, the shotgun raised, the charge fired, the young man pitching face down. These become effective in feature-style crime pieces and human-interest accounts, but should not sacrifice accuracy for drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include official statements, statistics, and resource information
rubrics_metrics.description: When relevant, report official figures and statements about institutional capacity or response (police force numbers, beat coverage, department comments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Little Italy piece quotes Chief Larry Ghent and gives numbers ('only four patrolmen', '264 patrolmen') to explain patterns of crime and response. Use such statistics to provide systemic context and attribution to named officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronicle series or pattern of incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple related incidents exist, present a concise chronology or list that shows frequency, dates, victims, and perpetrators to reveal a pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'MURDER IN LITTLE ITALY Since January 1' followed by dated entries. A chronological list can precede narrative analysis to show scope and repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report procedural and follow-up actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe legal and administrative steps following the incident: arrests, arraignments, commitments, hospital status updates, coroner actions, detentions without bail, wired inquiries to other jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Grew 'was arrested', 'ordered committed to jail for ten days', 'committed to jail'; coroner holding a suspect without bail; police wiring Arkansas authorities for a suspect. Follow-up clarity helps readers understand consequences and the status of justice processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include human-interest and family reaction material
rubrics_metrics.description: Use statements and anecdotes from relatives and acquaintances to humanize victims and show personal impact—while clearly attributing subjective remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The long account by Gene's mother gives emotional context and small personal details (dance steps, 'Happy Sheehan'). Such material should be balanced with factual reporting and attributed accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify suspects, capture narratives, and method of apprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Report on who is suspected, how they were pursued or captured, and any notable tactics or chance events leading to arrest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture of the escaped convict shows step-by-step apprehension—recognition of prison garb, constable intervention, 'Hands up!'—useful for telling the resolution story and crediting those involved in the capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention legal charges and relevant statutes when applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify the charges brought and any named statutes or federal laws that apply to the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example heading 'VIOLATION OF MANN ACT' and later description of arrest under the Mann Act. Identifying the law clarifies the nature and severity of the charge for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise identifying details (addresses, ages, occupations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide concrete identifying information—street addresses, ages, occupations, business names—so readers can place parties and verify facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the text: 'No. 21 Park street', '516-18 East Tenth Street', ages like '24 years old', occupations such as 'proprietor of the Neopolitan Macaroni factory'. Such specifics improve credibility and utility of the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize events chronologically to guide the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure the narrative in time order—lead with the key fact and then proceed through sequence of events, reactions, and official responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The vignettes proceed from encounter or discovery to police response, hospital/coroner outcome, and then background or reaction. Clear chronology prevents confusion and helps comprehension.
